title: The colour of light
teaches: Colour temperature, what white balance is guessing, the hours of the day as different kinds of light, and what a polariser does

blocks.text: **The challenge.** You stand at the edge of the same snowy park twice in one day. At noon the snow is white and the shadows of the trees are thin blue lines. Twenty minutes after sunset the whole field has turned a cold, luminous blue, the most beautiful it has looked all day. You take the picture, and the camera hands back the left-hand one: a flat grey field, the blue scrubbed out. What you saw, and wanted, is the right-hand one.

blocks.caption: The same snowy park at blue hour, as auto white balance saw it and as you did

blocks.text: The camera did what it is built to do: it decided the snow ought to be white and removed whatever colour the light was giving it. Most of the time that is a good idea, though at blue hour the colour of the light is the picture.[^blue-shadow]

Daylight is not one colour. Candlelight is orange, a household lamp yellowish, the noon sun nearly white, an overcast sky a little blue, and shade on a clear day, lit only by the blue sky, distinctly blue. Our eyes and brain adjust to each so quickly that we hardly notice; a white sheet of paper looks white under all of them. A camera's sensor does not adjust, and records the light as it is.

Photographers describe the colour of light by its **colour temperature**, in kelvin. The name comes from physics: a hot object glows, first red, then orange, then white, then bluish as it gets hotter, and the temperature that would glow a given colour labels it.[^kelvin] The confusing part is that this runs opposite to the way we talk about colour. "Warm" orange light is the low number, around 1900 K for a candle; "cool" blue light is the high one, 8000 K and up for blue shade.

blocks.caption: The colour of the light in places a nature photographer stands
blocks.task: Slide down to the colour of a lamp indoors, under 2800 K

blocks.text: **White balance** is the camera's guess at the colour of the light, which it then cancels out. Tell it the light is 5500 K and it leaves noon sunlight alone; tell it 3000 K and it adds blue to cancel the orange it expects. On automatic, it looks at the picture and guesses, usually by assuming the scene ought to average out neutral. At noon on snow that guess works, because the light is white and so is the snow. At blue hour it is right in the wrong way: the light really is blue, so it cancels the blue.

blocks.caption: A snowy park lit by noon sun, shade, or the sky after sunset, and the camera's white balance
blocks.task: In blue-hour light, set the white balance near daylight so the blue stays

blocks.text: The fix is to take white balance off automatic and tell the camera a fixed light: the **Daylight** preset (about 5500 K) records every light as it really differs from noon sun, so blue hour stays blue and a sunset stays orange. Set the kelvin setting lower than the light and the picture goes bluer still; set it higher and it warms up. White balance is a choice about mood as much as accuracy: for a heron's grey plumage at dusk you may want neutral, and for the field around it, the blue.

Light changes through the day in its colour, direction and hardness at once. When the sun is high the light is white and comes from above, so shadows are short and hard-edged, and birds get a dark band under the eye and a bright crown. As the sun drops, its light passes through more air, which scatters the blue out of it, so it turns golden, and it comes in low and sideways, raking across textures and lighting a bird's face.

blocks.caption: A tree on a snowy field as the sun climbs and sets
blocks.task: Lower the sun into the golden hour, under 6° above the horizon

blocks.text: The **golden hour** is the time when the sun is less than about six degrees above the horizon, roughly the first and last hour of sunlight. The **blue hour** is the twenty minutes or so after sunset or before sunrise, when there is no direct sun at all and everything is lit by the glowing sky. **Overcast** light is a third kind: the whole sky becomes one huge, soft lamp, a little blue, with almost no shadows. Photographers often grumble about grey days, but for birds in trees overcast is excellent, leaving no hard shadows or blown-out white feathers, and keeping colours rich rather than bleached.

Most advice says to keep the sun behind you so it lights the side of the bird you see. That is a safe start. With a low sun in front of you, though, light can come through the edges of the feathers and outline the whole bird in a bright rim, or turn a spread wing translucent. These are some of the most striking bird pictures there are, and they need two things.

First, keep the sun itself out of the frame, or just behind the bird, and shade the front of the lens with a hand or the lens hood to stop flare. Second, the meter will be thrown by the bright background, as in the lesson Light, and the three ways to let it in. Decide what you are exposing for, and use exposure compensation to nudge the camera's exposure darker or brighter: for a glowing rim, dial in minus compensation until the rim is bright but not clipped and let the rest go dark; for the bird's face, dial in plus and let the sky go white.

A **polarising filter** is the one filter whose effect cannot be done later on a computer. Light vibrates across its direction of travel, and some light, after scattering off air or reflecting off water and leaves, vibrates mainly in one direction: it is polarised. A polariser is a grid that passes light vibrating one way and blocks light vibrating the other. Turn it in its mount, and you choose which.

Blue sky is polarised most strongly at 90 degrees from the sun, and hardly at all toward the sun or straight away from it, so a polariser can darken it there, making clouds stand out. Glare off water and wet leaves is polarised too, horizontally, so the filter can cut it, letting you see into a stream or bringing back the green of shiny leaves. With the sun low and to one side, the two are polarised at right angles to each other, so you have to choose which to cut.[^polariser-stops]

blocks.caption: A lake with the sun low and to your left, through a polarising filter
blocks.task: Turn the filter to darken the sky, then to see into the water

blocks.text: Polarisers cost about a stop and a half of light, which matters at the long end, so they are mainly a close-up and wide-scene tool on the P950. At 24 mm the sky covers so wide an angle that only part of it is 90 degrees from the sun, and a polariser can leave a dark band across an otherwise even sky. Turn it until it looks right in the viewfinder, rather than to the strongest setting.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Colour temperature in kelvin runs low for warm light and high for blue shade.
Auto white balance cancels the colour of the light toward neutral.
The Daylight preset keeps the colour of golden and blue hour.
Sun angle and cloud set the colour, direction and hardness of light.
A polariser cuts glare or darkens blue sky 90° from the sun.

items.question: Which light has the higher colour temperature in kelvin?
options: Blue shade on a clear day
Candlelight
A household lamp
The sun just after rising
items.why: Blue light is the high number on the kelvin scale, around 8000 K for shade; orange candlelight is about 1900 K. The scale runs opposite to the everyday words warm and cool.

items.question: A sunset over a lake comes out pale and grey on auto white balance. What will bring the colour back?
options: Set white balance to the Daylight preset
Raise the ISO
Set white balance to the Shade preset
Narrow the aperture
items.why: Auto white balance cancels the orange it sees. Daylight records the light as it differs from noon sun, so the sunset stays orange. Shade would warm it even further, which may be too much.

items.question: Why are shadows on snow blue on a sunny day?
options: They are lit only by the blue sky
Snow absorbs red light in the shade
The camera's white balance makes them blue
Ice crystals in shadows are blue
items.why: Where the sun cannot reach, the only light is from the sky, which is blue. Our eyes partly ignore it; the camera does not.

items.question: Why is the light warm in the golden hour?
options: Low sun shines through more air, which scatters blue
The sun itself burns cooler in the evening hours
Dust in the air only rises in the evening
The camera's sensor warms up over the day
items.why: When the sun is low its light crosses much more atmosphere, and air scatters blue light more than red, leaving the direct sunlight orange and gold.

items.question: Your polariser does nothing to the sky when you face directly away from the sun. Why?
options: Skylight there is barely polarised
Polarisers only work on water
The filter must be turned past 90°
The sun has to be in the frame
items.why: Skylight is most strongly polarised at about 90° from the sun and hardly at all toward or directly away from it, so turning the filter there changes little.

items.question: For a bird in leafy trees, why can an overcast day be better than bright sun?
options: Soft, even light without hard shadows
Overcast light is warmer than sunlight
Birds sit more still on cloudy days
The camera can use a faster shutter then
items.why: Cloud turns the whole sky into a big soft light. Shadows under leaves and across the bird's face fade, and white feathers keep their detail, at the cost of some light.

summary: **Light has a colour, given in kelvin.** Candle about 1900 K, noon sun 5500 K, blue shade 8000 K and up; warm is the low number.
**White balance cancels the colour it thinks the light has.** On auto it pushes everything toward neutral.
**Fix white balance to keep a mood.** The Daylight preset keeps blue hour blue and sunsets orange.
**The time of day sets three things at once.** Colour, direction and hardness: low sun is warm and raking, high sun white and hard.
**Overcast is good light for birds.** Soft and even, with no hard shadows or blown whites.
**Backlight needs a decision.** Expose for the rim, darkening the rest, or for the face, letting the sky go white.
**A polariser is the filter software cannot copy.** It darkens blue sky 90° from the sun and cuts glare; turn it, and look.

blue-shadow.title: Why the sky is blue and snow shadows too
blue-shadow.text: Air molecules scatter short, blue wavelengths far more than long, red ones (Rayleigh scattering, which goes as the inverse fourth power of the wavelength). So the sky away from the sun glows blue, and anything lit only by the sky, such as a shadow on snow or the whole park after sunset, is lit blue. The same scattering takes the blue out of low sunlight, which is why the sun turns orange near the horizon.

kelvin.title: Lord Kelvin's scale
kelvin.text: Named after William Thomson, Lord Kelvin, who worked out the absolute temperature scale in the 1840s. It starts at absolute zero, so 5500 K is about 5200 °C, roughly the temperature of the sun's visible surface. Numbers above 8000 K describe skylight by the temperature a glowing body would need to look as blue.

polariser-stops.title: Linear and circular polarisers
polariser-stops.text: Most polarisers sold today are circular polarisers, which add a second layer behind the polarising one so that the camera's metering and autofocus, which can be confused by polarised light, keep working. On the P950 either kind works. The filter screws onto the front of the lens and rotates in its mount.
